items.title: Numerical reasoning: percentages and fractions
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Many Civil Service roles use online tests, usually multiple choice and against the clock. The numerical test asks you to work with percentages, fractions, ratios, averages and figures in tables. To find a percentage of a number, divide by 100 and multiply: 10% of 250 is 25. To reduce a number by a percentage, subtract the percentage amount: a £60 item reduced by 25% saves £15 and costs £45. For a fraction of a number, divide by the bottom and multiply by the top. When a question has several steps, do them in order and write each result down. Check the invitation to see whether a calculator is allowed. Practise until the basic sums are quick, then practise reading the question carefully so you answer what is asked.

questions.prompt: A £60 item is reduced by 25%. What is the new price?
40 people apply for a role and 3/8 of them are invited to interview. How many are invited?
A campaign receives 1,200 applications. 15% are rejected for missing information, then 40% of the remaining applications are sifted out. How many applications remain?

items.title: Numerical reasoning: averages, ratios and change
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: The mean (average) is the total divided by how many values there are. A ratio splits a total into parts: if letters and emails are in the ratio 3:2, then out of every 5 items 3 are letters and 2 are emails, so divide the total by 5 first and then multiply. Percentage changes in a row do not simply add up. A rise of 20% followed by a fall of 25% is applied to different starting amounts, so work through each step with the new figure. In a table or chart question, find the right row and column before you calculate, and watch the units (pounds or thousands, months or years). If you are stuck on one question, make your best estimate and move on, because every question usually carries the same mark.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 4, 6, 8 and 10?
A call centre took this many calls: Monday 30, Tuesday 45, Wednesday 25, Thursday 50, Friday 50. What is the mean number of calls per day?
Letters and emails are handled in the ratio 3:2. There are 60 items in total. How many are emails?
A team handled 200 cases in year one. In year two the number rose by 20%. In year three it fell by 25% from year two. How many cases did it handle in year three?

items.title: Verbal reasoning: true, false or cannot say
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: A verbal reasoning question gives you a short passage and a statement, and asks whether the statement is true, false or you cannot say. The rule is to use only the passage and ignore what you know or think is likely. True means the passage clearly says so or it follows directly. False means the passage clearly says the opposite. Cannot say means the passage does not give enough information to decide. The most common mistake is to choose true or false because the statement seems sensible, when the passage never says it. Watch for words such as all, most, never and caused. 'Most' is not a number the passage gave you. 'Caused' is a stronger claim than 'happened after'.

questions.prompt:
Passage: The office opens at 8am and closes at 6pm on weekdays. Visitors must sign in at reception. Staff may work from home for up to two days a week, if their line manager agrees.

Statement: Visitors must sign in at reception.

Passage: The office opens at 8am and closes at 6pm on weekdays. Visitors must sign in at reception. Staff may work from home for up to two days a week, if their line manager agrees.

Statement: Staff may work from home for as many days as they like.

Passage: The office opens at 8am and closes at 6pm on weekdays. Visitors must sign in at reception. Staff may work from home for up to two days a week, if their line manager agrees.

Statement: Most staff choose to work from home two days a week.

Passage: A review found that call waiting times fell after the new phone system was introduced. Customer satisfaction scores stayed the same.

Statement: The new phone system caused call waiting times to fall.

items.title: Situational judgement tests
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: A situational judgement test describes a work scenario and lists several possible responses. You are usually asked to choose the most effective response, and sometimes also the least effective. There is no hidden trick. The best response is usually the one that follows the Civil Service Code and the behaviours in the advert: honest, fair, safe, helpful, calm, and willing to ask for help or escalate when something is beyond your role. Weak responses ignore the problem, blame someone, cut corners, hide mistakes or act beyond your authority. Read every option before you choose. Think about what a good colleague who cares about the customer, the team and the rules would do.

questions.prompt: In a situational judgement test, what are you usually asked to do?

options.text: Choose the most effective response to a work scenario

questions.prompt: You are finishing an urgent task due in an hour when a colleague asks for help with something that is not urgent. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Drop your task and help at once
Explain your deadline, offer to help afterwards and suggest someone else if they need help sooner
Tell them it is not your job

questions.prompt: You notice that a letter you sent yesterday gave the wrong date for a customer's appointment. What is the most effective action?

options.text: Hope the customer does not notice
Quietly change your own copy only
Tell your manager straight away and follow the procedure to correct it with the customer
Wait to see whether anyone complains

questions.prompt: Two customers contact you at the same time. One wants a routine update on a form. The other says their payment has not arrived and they have no money for food this week. How do you prioritise and why?
questions.answer: Deal first with the customer in urgent need, following your department's procedure for vulnerable customers or hardship, which may mean getting urgent help from a manager or specialist team. Acknowledge the routine customer briefly, tell them you will come back to them by a set time, and then do so. Record what you did and why. This shows Managing a Quality Service and care for the customer, and the Civil Service Code's fairness: priority by need, not by who asked first.
questions.rubric: Should prioritise the urgent welfare need, follow or ask about procedure and escalate, acknowledge and follow up with the other customer, and keep a record.
